extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, historians, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles about how democratic social conditions shape armies, war, discipline, and political institutions; useful for political analysis or comparative military-political studies. Focuses on characteristics, causes, and consequences of democratic versus aristocratic military organization and behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of compulsory enlistment on soldier attachment
rubrics_metrics.description: When military service is compulsory in democratic nations, military service is temporary for most citizens: each citizen remains only a few years on active duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because service is common to all and brief, soldiers do not adopt the military profession as a permanent vocation; they retain ties to civil life and bring civilian habits and public opinion into the army. This contrasts with aristocratic systems where the military career is lifelong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private soldiers as conservative element reflecting society
rubrics_metrics.description: Private soldiers in democratic armies remain most like civilians and are the best carriers of the nation's manners, public opinion, and love of freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private soldiers' civilian attachments make them more amenable to inculcated national principles (freedom/respect of rights). If the general population is enlightened and energetic, private soldiers will help keep the army within bounds of order; if the population is ignorant/weak, soldiers can be drawn into disturbances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers' separation from civil life and warlike tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers in democratic armies often sever ties with civil life, owe their status to the army, and may see the army as their true country, which can make them more disposed toward war or revolutionary action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, top commanders may be the least warlike because many who rise from low origins to officer rank have secured inalienable advantages and may fear risking them. Thus chief commanders often prefer stability while certain officers may favor conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-commissioned officers as most warlike/revolutionary class
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-commissioned officers occupy an intermediate social/military position and are predisposed to be the most warlike and revolutionary element within democratic armies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They have broken ties with civilian life and are permanently devoted to service but lack secure, high rank. Their precarious status, thwarted hopes for promotion, exposure to privations, and constant dependence on superiors kindle desperate ambition; they may favor war or revolution to overturn established authority and seize promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic armies weaker at the outset after long peace
rubrics_metrics.description: After a long peace democratic armies are especially vulnerable at the start of a campaign: soldiers tend to be young/inexperienced while leading officers tend to be old and lack vigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes include the rule of seniority, slow promotion, and the social tendency for the best minds to avoid military careers in peacetime. This age/experience split undermines initial generalship and competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long peace produces habits and institutional inertia unfit for war
rubrics_metrics.description: Peace induces habits of body and mind among officers and men that make them ill-adapted to the rigors of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officers accustomed to calm civil life may be unable to adapt to the toils and stern duties of warfare; slowness of promotion and contentment with security further reduce wartime readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protracted war transforms democratic armies into formidable forces
rubrics_metrics.description: While weak at first, democratic armies grow more formidable the longer a war continues because war mobilizes the nation, attracts ambitious and talented individuals, and opens rapid paths to advancement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long wars break regulations, create vacancies through death, and allow extraordinary men to rise quickly. The principle of equality permits wide competition for honors, accelerating the selection of energetic young leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical strength becomes decisive in democratic warfare
rubrics_metrics.description: As nations become similar (socially and militarily), the qualitative superiority of special troops declines and victory increasingly depends on sheer numerical strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When soldiers are largely interchangeable in skill, the largest army has the advantage; small nations must join larger states or be absorbed because numbers determine outcomes more than unique troop types.

rubrics_metrics.name: State capacity enables mass mobilisation in democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic states, with strong central power and the desire to enroll large portions of the male population, are able to mobilize mass armies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because citizens are more alike and individually weaker, the state concentrates power and can raise greater numbers, matching the new military requirement for mass forces despite citizens' general aversion to war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern tactics favor decisive battles and seizure of capitals
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary modes of war (as exemplified by Napoleon) favor rapid, decisive engagements and marching upon enemy capitals to end wars quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shift suits democratic nations capable of bringing whole disposable forces into the field; such tactics capitalize on centralization and numerical mobilization rather than prolonged feudal-style sieges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability of democratic nations due to lack of local resistance centres
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic nations are more vulnerable to conquest because, absent strong local/noble centers of resistance, the capture of the capital can paralyze the nation and end organized resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike aristocratic countries where nobles provide pockets of resistance, democratic populations lack local rallying points; provincial liberties and powers can mitigate but not fully correct this vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline in democracies should direct not annihilate free faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of military discipline exist: aristocratic (blind, minute obedience) and democratic (directed obedience rooted in the will and reason of soldiers); democratic discipline should not try to destroy soldiers' freedom of thought but to channel it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democratic armies cannot and should not aim for slavish obedience; instead cultivate obedience that rests on soldiers' judgment and patriotism, which may become stricter voluntarily when danger requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic discipline strengthens under fire; aristocratic discipline can relax
rubrics_metrics.description: Discipline founded on habit (aristocratic) tends to break down in war, whereas discipline that depends on soldiers' will and understanding (democratic) is likely to strengthen when facing the enemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because democratic soldiers understand the stakes and choose obedience rationally, they often exhibit more eager and intelligent obedience in combat than habitually obedient troops whose habits are disturbed by war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership by example and converse maintains order in democratic armies
rubrics_metrics.description: In armies of freemen (ancient democracies), fraternal familiarity between officers and soldiers, leadership by language and example, kept troops in order more effectively than constraint or punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Greece and Rome, Plutarch) show officers who listened and answered soldiers and maintained discipline through companionship and moral example rather than coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spread of equality reduces propensity to initiate wars but widens their scope
rubrics_metrics.description: When equality spreads across neighboring nations, inhabitants grow alike in tastes and interests, leading to a shared dread of war (making wars rarer) but making any war that does occur likely to embroil multiple states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic interdependence and similarity of interests make nations reluctant to wage war, but if war occurs it tends to spread because harms inflicted on one will rebound on others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small states pressured to incorporate or align due to numeric determinism
rubrics_metrics.description: Because numerical strength predominates in democratic-era warfare, smaller nations are compelled to join larger states or follow their policy; numerical majorities determine victory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical contrasts (e.g., Helvetic Confederacy) show that when surrounding states are alike, only population size differentiates power, forcing small states to adopt incorporation or alignment strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil wars less frequent and less protracted in democratic ages absent army split
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic populations are less prone to protracted civil war because they lack entrenched subordinate powers and trusted leaders to coordinate resistance; a civil war would likely be short unless the army itself splits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful internal revolutions by force require seizing the state's machinery quickly; prolonged civil wars occur mainly when the armed forces divide into factions, otherwise the majority state power quashes resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality inclines citizens toward free institutions and elected government
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of equality fosters a taste for independence and political freedom; citizens naturally prefer institutions where leaders are elected and administration is subject to their control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because equality makes individuals jealous of authority, they are predisposed to value and pursue representative/elected forms of government. The loss of a strong supreme power risks disorder, but the primary democratic tendency is toward free institutions.
